section_summary: This section contains diplomatic reporting and press commentaries from China regarding the February 26, 1936 military coup d'état in Tokyo, during which ultra-nationalist junior army officers assassinated leading Japanese government figures including Finance Minister Korekiyo Takahashi and Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Makoto Saito. It includes newspaper clippings from English-language journals in Shanghai transmitted by Consul General C. E. Gauss (Despatch No. 51), a State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing diplomatic reports from China, and Despatch No. 283 from the American Embassy in Peiping forwarding translations of Chinese vernacular editorials. The commentators and analysts examine the underlying causes of the mutiny, linking it to the court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa, ideological agitation for a 'Showa Restoration', and acute factional rivalries within the Japanese military between the Controlling and Imperial Way cliques.

subfiles.about: Enclosures to Shanghai Despatch No. 51 transmitting editorial clippings from English-language newspapers in Shanghai on the February 26 military insurrection in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Consul General at Shanghai
subfiles.summary: This subfile comprises press clippings forwarded as enclosures to Despatch No. 51 by American Consul General C. E. Gauss in Shanghai concerning the Tokyo military rebellion of February 26, 1936. The clippings—from the Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury, The China Press, The North-China Daily News, and The Shanghai Times—analyze the roots of the coup, connecting it to the sensational trial of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa for the murder of General Nagata and the growth of an assassination cult in the military. They report the murders of Finance Minister Takahashi and former Prime Minister Saito, the narrow escapes of Prince Saionji and Count Makino, and the financial pressures caused by escalating military expenditures. The editorials express deep foreboding that if ultra-militarists prevail, Japan will face international isolation and continental conflagration.
subfiles.title: Sino-Japanese Relations: Shanghai Opinion on February 26 Incident (Despatch No. 51 Enclosures)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing diplomatic despatches from Peiping, Nanking, and Shanghai on Chinese and foreign press reactions to the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State (EHD, JCV, VDM)
subfiles.summary: This memorandum drafted in the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs provides a comparative digest of three diplomatic despatches forwarding press commentaries on the Tokyo uprising: Peiping's Despatch No. 283, Nanking's Despatch No. 123, and Shanghai's Despatch No. 51. It highlights Chinese vernacular press sentiment hoping Japan will address internal stability rather than foreign expansion, notes one Japanese-controlled Chinese-language paper welcoming military dictatorship and an active China policy, and outlines English-language editorial criticism from Shanghai focusing on the Aizawa trial and runaway militarism.
subfiles.title: Press Comment on the Tokyo Incident of February 26

subfiles.about: Despatch No. 283 from the American Embassy in Peiping transmitting English translations of Chinese vernacular newspaper editorials on the Tokyo coup d'état.
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, Counselor of Embassy (for the Ambassador), American Embassy, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy F. P. Lockhart transmits translations of editorials published on February 27 and 28, 1936 in Peiping and Tientsin vernacular newspapers concerning the Tokyo military rebellion. The editorial from the pro-Japanese Asia Peoples' Voice characterizes the coup as the dawn of 'Showa Modernization' against corrupt party politicians and plutocrats, urging military dictatorship and an active continental policy. In contrast, independent papers like Ta Kung Pao urge Japanese authorities to prioritize domestic economic and political reform over foreign expansion, while Shih Chieh Jih Pao provides an extensive structural analysis of the factional struggle inside the Japanese Army between the Controlling Clique (led by Hayashi) and the Youth/Imperial Way Clique (led by Araki).
subfiles.title: Peiping Press Comment on the Military Disturbance of February 26 at Tokyo (Despatch No. 283)
